summary: Gives guidelines for using XML in IETF protocols. XML has become a widely used way of representing structured data, and many protocols need such a representation. This Best Current Practice discusses when XML is appropriate and what to consider when designing with it.

eli5.summary: Many Internet rules need a way to write down organized data. This note advises rule writers on when and how to use XML for it.

questions: when to use xml in a protocol
when should a protocol use xml
which media type should xml protocols use
subtitle: BCP 70: when XML fits inside a protocol, and the design choices to make once you pick it.

tldr.problem: Many Internet protocols need a way to represent structured data, and XML had become a popular choice, but its many optional features can be used badly inside a protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC weighs XML against alternatives such as ASN.1, XDR and ABNF, then gives recommendations on well-formedness, declarations, validity, namespaces, binary data, white space, character encoding, IANA and security.
tldr.outcome: It became BCP 70, IETF policy for XML in standards-track protocols. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3470 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 70) and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Extensible Markup Language (XML) is a framework for structuring data. It grew out of SGML, which focused on documents, and has become a widely used way to represent structured data in protocol exchanges. This BCP is a guide to XML usage and also IETF policy for standards-track documents.

The scope is narrow. The goal is not to say XML is the best or preferred representation, but to lay out how to use it inside a larger protocol once other factors point to XML. The Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP) is given as an example of a protocol these guidelines would cover. The RFC does not cover sending XML documents as ordinary email or web content, protocols built entirely on XML such as the W3C's SOAP-based framework, or higher-level XML frameworks such as RDF.

XML 1.0 was published as a W3C recommendation in February 1998 and revised in a second edition in October 2000. The RFC refers to that second edition.
sections.eli5: This guide is not saying everyone must use XML. It says: if you have already decided to use it, here is how to do it well.

sections.title: Is XML the Right Tool?
sections.content:
Section 2 lists thirteen factors to weigh. On the positive side, XML is a meta-markup language for defining markup languages for specific domains, framing is built in, instances can be validated against a formal definition, it supports internationalization, new tags can be added without changing XML itself, and it is text-based, so fragments are easy to create, edit, debug and log. Support is available in many software utilities, both open source and proprietary.

On the cost side, XML has no native detailed data typing, binary data must be encoded as text, and XML is verbose compared with many other representations. Processing can be slower because streams are larger and a general-purpose parser adds a layer, and some processing requires examining every byte. The RFC also says XML was still evolving and its implementations were still relatively new, so defects in early and current products were not unusual.
sections.eli5: XML is easy to read and easy to extend, but it takes more space and more time to process than a tightly packed format. You weigh the good against the cost.

sections.title: XML Compared with Other Representations
sections.content:
For many fundamental protocols the extensibility needs are modest and the performance needs high, so fixed binary data blocks are the appropriate choice, and XML would merely add bloat. The RFC points to RFC 3252 as a humorous example of XML as protocol bloat.

It compares XML with three alternatives: ASN.1 with its Basic Encoding Rules (used in SNMP and other standards), XDR (used for example by NFS), and BNF or ABNF (used for example by SMTP). The differences it highlights are text encoding and character sets, data encoding, extensibility and legibility.

XML defines a character model based on the Universal Character Set, requires parsers to accept at least UTF-8 and UTF-16, and has a rich extensibility model, although it has no standard way to say whether an extension is mandatory to recognize. ASN.1 and XDR use binary encodings that are not easily human readable, and XDR is not independently extensible by different parties because its framing and data types are implicit.
sections.eli5: There are other ways to write down data. Some are compact but hard for people to read; XML is easy to read but bulkier.

sections.title: Syntax, Declarations, Instructions and Comments
sections.content:
An instance is XML if and only if it is well-formed. Without that, all the advantages of XML disappear, so protocol specifications should explicitly require it (MUST be well-formed). This seems at odds with the IETF tradition of being liberal in what you accept, but the RFC is firm: a protocol must never recommend partially interpreting non-well-formed XML. Reasonable reactions are to retransmit or to abort the session.

The RFC advises against syntactic restrictions that subset XML, such as banning CDATA sections or character entity references, because implementers could then no longer use an ordinary conforming XML processor. Where tight control is truly needed, designers should consider Canonical XML (RFC 3076). Defining a protocol element only by its abstract Information Set, while allowing other concrete syntaxes, is out of scope.

An XML declaration such as <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> states the XML version and character encoding. It SHOULD be present and MAY always be sent, and it should be required when the encoding is anything other than UTF-8 or UTF-16.

Processing instructions are recommended to be ignored in normal protocol processing and not used to define normative data structures, because they are not namespace aware, most schema languages cannot constrain them, and they have no structure beyond a target and the rest. Comments can be ignored by conformant processors, so it is strongly recommended that they not define normative structures and be ignored too.
sections.eli5: If a message is not written exactly by the rules, throw it out instead of guessing what it meant. Notes and side instructions tucked into a message should be ignored, so never hide important rules in them.

sections.title: Validity, Semantics, Namespaces and Element Design
sections.content:
Several formalisms can define what a valid instance looks like: DTDs, XML Schema, and others such as Schematron and RELAX NG. Protocols should use an appropriate one. They may or may not insist that every element be valid, but the extensibility design should be clear, including what happens if data is not valid. Because XML has no standard way to say whether an extension is mandatory to recognize, specifications should describe their extension mechanisms and whether extensions must be recognized or ignored. Implementations may skip run-time validation and rely on hand-written code.

A formal definition is not enough: XML supplies no semantics, so any document defining a protocol element with XML MUST also describe its semantics in prose.

Namespaces let elements from different vocabularies with the same name be told apart and support extensibility. Protocols should reuse existing namespaces where appropriate. A new namespace name is a URI, preferably persistent and pointing to a description. For IETF documents, URNs in the IETF URN namespace can serve, and creating new URI schemes to define XML namespaces is strongly discouraged. An unprefixed attribute belongs to no namespace, not to the default namespace.

When designing elements and attributes, remember that attributes are unordered, can appear only once per element, cannot contain internal markup, and have their values normalized. Consistent use of elements, attributes and values is a mark of sound design. Enumerated values should come with a plan to extend them: revise the protocol, use different namespaces, or set up an IANA registry. The use of default attribute values is discouraged, because it hurts software that does not know the validity constraints, for example in packet tracing or digital signatures.
sections.eli5: Give every kind of label its own family name so two labels never get confused. Always explain in plain words what each label means, and say how new labels may be added later.

sections.title: Binary Data, White Space, Entities and Character Sets
sections.content:
XML is a character stream, so raw binary data cannot be embedded. It must be encoded, for example as Base64 or hexadecimal digits, or sent over another channel and referenced by URI. Protocols that need to hold large quantities of binary data should consider carefully whether XML is appropriate, since those encodings are inefficient, and Base64 is best for larger amounts. XML also forbids most control characters, even through character references, so text that is fine in an ABNF-defined protocol may need to be treated as binary in XML.

Other recommendations:

  • Avoid entity declarations in protocol specifications, since they add complexity and suit documents better than data. The five built-in entity references and numeric character references should be allowed.
  • Do not let the meaning of a message depend on information outside it, such as external entities, particularly in stateless protocols.
  • If xml:base is allowed, specify how it interacts with other ways of setting URI context. Say clearly which characters a URI may contain, as most IETF protocols do not allow non-ASCII characters there.
  • All white space in XML instances is significant and visible to applications, so protocols should give specific guidance on how to handle it.
  • Incremental processing of XML as tags arrive can be hard if it must span both directions of a bidirectional stream.

On character sets, XML works in terms of the Universal Character Set and requires processors to support UTF-8 and UTF-16. This RFC requires that IETF protocols using XML allow UTF-8, and recommends also allowing UTF-16 with its Byte Order Mark. Any other encoding must be named in the XML declaration. Protocols carrying human-language text are strongly recommended to mandate the xml:lang attribute when the content may be used in language-dependent contexts.
sections.eli5: XML only carries text, so pictures or other raw data must be turned into letters first, which makes them bigger. Pick one common alphabet code, UTF-8, so everybody can read everybody else's words.

sections.title: Media Types and IANA
sections.content:
The memo itself has no impact on IANA, but using XML in a protocol may need IANA action. If the XML has no meaning outside its original protocol context, there is no reason to register a MIME type. If it could be interpreted elsewhere, such as when stored in a file system or tunneled over another protocol, a type can be registered. Following RFC 3023, a new language or document type should get a new media type. For generic structured data, application/xml MAY be used, while text/xml SHOULD NOT be used, because of issues with display behavior and default character sets.

The RFC also mentions an ongoing effort to create a URN namespace for naming XML namespaces and other URI-designated protocol elements in IETF standards-track documents.
sections.eli5: If your XML message might travel outside its home protocol, give it a proper label saying what kind of thing it is, using the official list kept by IANA.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML has no built-in security services, but other layers can protect it. XML encryption provides privacy, Canonical XML and XML digital signatures provide integrity and authentication, and TLS protects data and endpoints. The RFC says protocol specifications must mandate additional security services to counter common threats, depending on the protocol's threat model.

Code that parses network traffic is often a soft target, so implementers MUST take great care that XML handling is robust against malformed XML, buffer overruns and misuse of entity declarations. Mechanisms that follow external references can cause an implementation to reach external resources automatically, so arbitrary access to such references from untrusted sources must be disallowed.
sections.eli5: XML does not lock anything by itself, so add locks from elsewhere. Be careful reading messages from strangers, and never automatically fetch whatever a stranger's message points to.
